idiom_name: synchronized (gate) blocks on a dedicated lock object
implementation_notes: Every Java object carries an intrinsic lock (monitor), so the object itself is what gets published: synchronized (obj) { ... } names the object that provides the lock, synchronized methods use this (or the Class object for static methods), and a released monitor establishes the happens-before relation that makes writes visible. The documented idiom for a lockable object is a dedicated lock object plus synchronized blocks; keep the lock private and expose either the object or a lock accessor deliberately, because publishing this hands the monitor to subclasses and foreign code.
pitfalls: synchronized(this) and synchronized methods publish the object's own monitor to subclasses and foreign code; use a dedicated final lock object when collaborators must take the lock.
Intrinsic locks are reentrant and uninterruptible: there is no timeout, no tryLock and no fairness control, so a blocked monitor can only be diagnosed, not bounded.
wait()/notify() require holding the matching monitor, belong in a while-loop around the predicate, and are unusable from outside if the lock is private.

A virtual thread that blocks inside a synchronized block can pin its carrier thread, which is a strong argument for j.u.c locks in virtual-thread deployments under contention (analysis, not a spec claim).

variants.name: Published Lock object from java.util.concurrent.locks
variants.idiom_name: ReentrantLock (or ReadWriteLock) published as a Lock
variants.implementation_notes: Since Java 5 the java.util.concurrent.locks framework offers locks that are distinct from built-in synchronization and monitors: the object holds a ReentrantLock (or a ReadWriteLock's pair), publishes it as a Lock, and each critical section does lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock(); }. The explicit lock adds what monitors cannot - tryLock with timeout, interruptible acquisition, fairness, per-lock Condition queues and non-block-structured use such as hand-over-hand locking - which is why the pattern's classic form maps naturally onto Lock when callers must hold several locks in a defined order or fail fast instead of blocking.
pitfalls: Lock has no implicit release: every path needs try/finally, because an exception between lock() and unlock() leaks the lock and stalls every other user.
Condition replaces wait/notify with a different API (await/signal, always inside the lock) - mixing Object.wait on the same monitor and a Condition on the same state creates two exclusion domains.
Reentrancy is per implementation: ReentrantLock may be re-entered, StampedLock must not be, and acquiring two published locks without tryLock timeouts converts a deadlock into a hang.
Fairness (new ReentrantLock(true)) trades throughput for starvation resistance; picking it by default without measurement is a common performance mistake.
